title: Mac and Dennis Break Up

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis repeatedly calling 'Dee. Dee. Dee. Sweet Dee.' in an escalating chant to get her attention for a popcorn bowl
jokes.setup: Two grown men have shown up at Dee's apartment together just to borrow a bowl
jokes.punchline: Their synchronized, increasingly insistent chanting of her name reveals how weirdly in-sync and codependent they already are before the episode's theme is even established
jokes.explanation: Works as a cold open because it immediately demonstrates the episode's thesis — these two men operate as one unit — before anyone has articulated it. The synchronized chanting is funnier than a single person calling her name. Good character integration.

dialogue.line: Multiple characters chanting 'Dee' and 'Sweet Dee' repeatedly before she responds with confusion

jokes.text: "Congratulations, Dee. You've begun your transformation into crazy cat lady."
jokes.setup: Dee explains she got a cat because she has no roommate and no one to talk to
jokes.punchline: Dennis's formal, mock-ceremonial congratulation framing loneliness as a transformation milestone
jokes.explanation: The word 'congratulations' does the heavy lifting — framing her sad admission as an achievement. Dennis's smug condescension is perfectly in character. The 'crazy cat lady' trope is well-worn but the delivery elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Congratulations, Dee. You've begun your transformation into crazy cat lady.

jokes.text: Dee's explanation for getting the cat: 'I just got a cat 'cause I wanted something to hang out with. I don't have a roommate or anything, and I don't really have anyone to talk to.'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to defend her cat as a normal, healthy choice
jokes.punchline: Her defense inadvertently confirms every sad thing about her life in a single sentence, undercutting herself completely
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP structure: character tries to defend themselves and only digs deeper. The comedy is in Dee's complete lack of self-awareness that she is proving Dennis right mid-sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I just got a cat... 'cause I wanted something to hang out with. I don't have, you know, a roommate or anything, and I don't really have anyone to talk to

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis explain they both came over just to get one bowl: Dennis was going to hold the bowl while Mac was going to stand next to him and make snide comments
jokes.setup: Dee asks why they both had to come over just to borrow a popcorn bowl
jokes.punchline: They reveal they've assigned themselves distinct roles for a task that requires zero collaboration — 'I was gonna hold the bowl. Dennis was gonna stand next to me and make snide comments.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The absurdity is pitch-perfect: they've formalized their codependency into professional roles for a mundane errand. 'I was gonna hold the bowl' / 'Dennis was gonna stand next to me and make snide comments' is deadpan genius. It perfectly illustrates the episode's thesis while being completely specific to these characters. The division of labor where one person's job is literally just to exist next to the other is a brilliant character joke. High quotability, strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: If you listen to yourself, you would realize you're only strengthening our argument.

jokes.text: "Oh, you look like a bird. That's one."
jokes.setup: Mac explains Dennis's role was to 'stand next to me and make snide comments'
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately demonstrates this by deploying a snide comment at Dee and numbering it like a sport
jokes.explanation: The 'bird' insult is a recurring joke in the series (Dee has been called a bird-like creature). The genius here is 'That's one' — Dennis is literally scorekeeping his insults. This demonstrates the insult routine is so practiced they've formalized it with numbers. High character integration, excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mac and Dennis movie night! Whoosh! Tuesday night's movie night! We're doing Predator again.

jokes.text: "If the two of us didn't come together, what if one of us were to get into a jam? Be silly not to have the other one there." Dennis: "Silly? Dennis, that sounds downright dangerous."
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining why both men were needed to pick up a popcorn bowl
jokes.punchline: Mac invokes the possibility of a 'jam' arising during a bowl-retrieval trip; Dennis escalates 'silly' to 'downright dangerous' as if they were on a Special Forces mission
jokes.explanation: The 'jam' language and Dennis escalating the stakes from 'silly' to 'dangerous' perfectly illustrates their self-mythology — they treat a bowl pickup like a tactical operation. Sets up the 'jam' callback that runs through the entire episode.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's more fun if we both come. I was gonna hold the bowl. Dennis was gonna stand next to me and make snide comments.

jokes.text: "See, you'll never get out of a jam because you got no friends. Well, you're a spinster." / "Mm-hmm. A lonely spinster. With a cat."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are defending their codependency by pointing out Dee has no one
jokes.punchline: They land on 'spinster' and then collaboratively layer on 'lonely' and 'with a cat' — a perfectly synchronized verbal beatdown delivered as a joint art project
jokes.explanation: The incremental building — spinster → lonely spinster → with a cat — demonstrates their perfect synchronization as a comedic duo, which ironically proves Dee's point about codependency. 'Those are all funny' from one of them is a nice meta-beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, you look like a bird. That's one. Uh... Old. Pick a new one.

jokes.text: "Those are all funny."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have just collaboratively piled on insults at Dee
jokes.punchline: One of them cheerfully grades their own insults as 'all funny' — meta-commentary on their own joke quality mid-scene
jokes.explanation: Three words that deliver a lot: self-satisfaction, obliviousness, and comedy-workshop energy. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: what if one of us were to get into a jam?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Be silly not to have the other one there.

jokes.text: Dee's reframing: "I feel like you guys are two codependent losers who are so wrapped up in each other that it's hard for you to see how pathetic your lives are. It's like you're an old married couple."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been defending their bowl-fetching partnership as logical and necessary
jokes.punchline: Dee articulates the episode's entire thesis in one speech — but crucially, she's right, and they can't see it
jokes.explanation: Functions as the inciting incident speech. The humor is in how correct she is and how completely they reject it. 'Old married couple' is the thesis statement of the episode. Functional but not especially inventive writing.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dennis, that sounds downright dangerous.

jokes.text: "No, Dee. We're more like a dynamic duo."
jokes.setup: Dee calls them an 'old married couple'
jokes.punchline: Dennis corrects her with 'dynamic duo' — which is simultaneously more grandiose and equally revealing of codependency
jokes.explanation: The correction from 'old married couple' to 'dynamic duo' is funny because both phrases describe the same relationship, but Dennis hears one as insulting and one as flattering. Tight economy.

dialogue.line: you'll never get out of a jam because you got no friends. Well, you're a spinster. A lonely spinster. With a cat.

jokes.text: The 'checking in' revelation: Dee asks when was the last time they went more than an hour without seeing each other. Dennis: 'All the time. Every day.' Mac: 'He always checks in with me.' Dennis: 'Yeah, yeah, yeah. He likes to have me check in, but it's not like—'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to prove Mac and Dennis are codependent by asking about their checking-in habits
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately outs Dennis as a chronic check-in-er; Dennis's attempted denial dissolves mid-sentence as he can't actually finish the exculpatory clause
jokes.explanation: The trailing 'it's not like—' is the punchline — Dennis literally cannot finish his defense because there is no defense. Mac blowing his cover is a perfect friend-betrayal beat. Character-specific and structurally clean.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It's funny 'cause I feel like you guys are two codependent losers... who are so wrapped up in each other... that it's hard for you to see how pathetic your lives are. It's like you're an old married couple.

jokes.text: "She doesn't know anything about friendship, dude. No. How could she? She doesn't have any friends."
jokes.setup: Dee has just correctly diagnosed their codependency and left
jokes.punchline: They immediately dismiss her accurate observation by pointing to her friendlessness — which they just spent the scene mocking — proving they heard nothing
jokes.explanation: Functional irony — the audience knows they're wrong, they don't. Standard sitcom beat but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, Dee. We're more like a dynamic duo.

jokes.text: Mac's panic attack: Dennis was gone for about an hour getting a movie and Mac texted '911' — an emergency code — because he couldn't get in touch with him
jokes.setup: Dennis returns from the video store after being gone roughly an hour
jokes.punchline: Mac reveals he texted 911 (their agreed emergency code), considered calling the police, and had been 'calling sort of over and over again' — all for a one-hour errand
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the 'checking in' setup. The fact that they have an agreed '911 = emergency' text protocol for a roommate situation, and that Mac was considering police involvement after one hour, is an escalation that lands hard. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: When was the last time you went more than an hour without seeing each other?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: All the time.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Every day.

jokes.text: Mac: "I almost called the police." Dennis: "I mean, that's a bit of an overreaction. I was gone for what, an hour?"
jokes.setup: Mac reveals he nearly called police after Dennis was gone for an hour
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'that's a bit of an overreaction' is the understatement of the century — he delivers it completely calmly, as if Mac calling the police over a one-hour errand is only slightly excessive
jokes.explanation: Slight underreaction to an overreaction. Dennis's calm framing of near-police-involvement as 'a bit of an overreaction' (not insane, not insane, just 'a bit') is a good deadpan beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Okay. Without checking in?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Ch... Checking. That's... Uh... huh.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He always checks in with me.

jokes.text: Mac's objection to The Transporter 2: "Plus, Transporter 2? We haven't seen Transporter 1, which means we'll be completely lost."
jokes.setup: Dennis has brought home The Transporter 2 instead of Predator
jokes.punchline: Mac's concern about being 'completely lost' without having seen Transporter 1 — as if Jason Statham action movies have deeply complex continuity that requires prior knowledge
jokes.explanation: Funny because it's exactly wrong — The Transporter is not a franchise requiring deep investment. Mac applies serious analytical thinking to a braindead action franchise. Very Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yo, where you been?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I was getting the movie.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, but you weren't answering any of my calls. I've been calling you... sort of over and over again.

jokes.text: "Plus Jason Statham's physique is nothing like the lineup in Predator."
jokes.setup: Mac is running through his objections to The Transporter 2
jokes.punchline: He invokes male physique comparison as a serious movie-selection criterion — specifically critiquing Statham against the Predator ensemble as if conducting a formal athletic assessment
jokes.explanation: One of Mac's most revealing and funny lines. His homoerotic fixation on male physique is a long-running character trait (Mac is closeted), and invoking it here as a legitimate film-selection criterion — presented with total seriousness — is excellent character comedy. The specific comparison to 'the lineup in Predator' makes it sharper.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I texted you 911, dude. That means it's an emergency.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What was the emergency, Mac?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, I couldn't get in touch with you, dude.

jokes.text: Dennis: "Okay, stop. I don't want to have conversations anymore about dudes' physiques." Mac: "Dennis, in body mass alone—" Dennis: "That's what I was trying to avoid... a conversation about body mass, okay? We've had that conversation five times a day for the last month."
jokes.setup: Mac invokes Jason Statham's physique deficiency vs. Predator cast
jokes.punchline: Dennis reveals they have had the body mass conversation five times a day for a month — the horror of their routine fully revealed
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'Mac likes physiques' to 'we have had this exact conversation 150 times over the past month' is what makes it land. Dennis's weary specificity ('five times a day for the last month') conveys the exhausted intimacy of a long relationship. Well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I almost called the police.

jokes.text: "No. You'd rather have conversations with video store clerks."
jokes.setup: Dennis says he doesn't want to talk about body mass anymore
jokes.punchline: Mac's jealous accusation about the video store clerk — framed as romantic betrayal — lands as a perfect 'old married couple' beat
jokes.explanation: Mac's jealousy over the video store clerk functions as a perfectly observed relationship insecurity beat. The substitution of 'another man' for a random clerk elevates the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Plus, Transporter 2? We haven't seen Transporter 1, which means we'll be completely lost.

jokes.text: "I have been thinking a lot about what Dee said, and I do think... maybe we are spending a little bit too much time together." — delivered with the gravity of a breakup speech
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have just had their first real fight about the movie
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers what is structurally a romantic breakup speech, complete with pauses for weight, about two male roommates who watch movies together
jokes.explanation: This is the structural centerpiece of the episode's comedy: a full romantic-breakup scene played completely straight between two men who insist they're just buddies. The pauses, the gravity, 'I do think...' — all of it is calibrated for maximum cringe. The commitment to the bit is what elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Plus Jason Statham's physique... is nothing like the lineup in Predator.

jokes.text: "I feel like I'm not... flourishing."
jokes.setup: Dennis is mid-breakup speech with Mac about their friendship
jokes.punchline: 'Flourishing' — the word arrives after a long pause and is both pompous and completely absurd in context, as if Dennis is a flower being denied sunlight by Mac
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The pause before 'flourishing' is load-bearing — it promises something emotionally significant and delivers something absurdly self-aggrandizing. Dennis's narcissism channeled through therapy-speak about not being allowed to 'flourish' is both hilarious and revealing. 'Well, far be it from me to keep the flower of you from flourishing' is a perfect response that acknowledges the absurdity while staying in-scene. Highly quotable, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We've had that conversation five times a day for the last month... because we keep watching Predator, and all you talk about is Weathers... and Jesse 'the Body' Ventura and how many pounds they can pack on.

jokes.text: Mac's response: "Well, far be it from me to, uh, keep the flower of you from flourishing, but, uh, I guess I'll grab my shit and stay at Charlie's."
jokes.setup: Dennis has used 'flourishing' as the climax of his breakup speech
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'keep the flower of you from flourishing' is hurt-but-dignified, the perfect wounded-partner response — before the mundane logistics of 'I'll grab my shit and stay at Charlie's' deflate it completely
jokes.explanation: Mac mirrors Dennis's elevated language ('flower of you from flourishing') which is funny because it means Mac also heard and internalized the absurd metaphor. The emotional callback lands. The 'grab my shit and stay at Charlie's' grounds it back in reality perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's important to pack on mass. You're talking about carbo-loading.

jokes.text: Post-'breakup' negotiation: who stays vs. who goes, culminating in Dennis arguing he should stay because 'I have more stuff. It'll take me longer to pack, and it'll be easier.'
jokes.setup: Mac says he'll go to Charlie's; Dennis says Mac doesn't have to do that; then Dennis says Mac already said he would, so Mac should go
jokes.punchline: Dennis's final justification is pure logistical self-interest: 'I have more stuff' — the breakup has degenerated into an apartment logistics dispute in seconds
jokes.explanation: The speed at which their romantic breakup scene devolves into 'I have more stuff' is very funny. It's a classic IASIP move: emotional sincerity immediately undercut by petty self-interest.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I have been thinking a lot about what Dee said, and I do think... maybe we are spending a little bit too much time together.

jokes.text: A police officer arrives at the door: "Hi. I'm responding to a missing persons report."
jokes.setup: Mac mentioned earlier that he 'almost called the police' when Dennis was gone for an hour
jokes.punchline: He did call the police — a missing persons report — for a man who had been away for one hour getting a movie
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Mac said 'I almost called the police' — and he actually did. The officer's deadpan 'I'm responding to a missing persons report' mid-breakup scene is a gem of timing and structure. The joke is entirely setup-dependent (it only lands if you remember the earlier line) which makes it rewarding for attentive viewers. Excellent structure and economy — one line does enormous comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I feel like I'm not... flourishing.

jokes.text: Dennis shows up at Dee's apartment after the 'breakup,' claiming he was inspired by her wisdom: "I wasn't spending enough time by myself. I wasn't being an independent individual. I wasn't flourishing."
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac have just 'broken up'; Dennis presents himself as having grown from Dee's advice
jokes.punchline: He immediately goes to Dee's apartment to watch a movie with her — replacing one companion with another within minutes, completely failing to understand what 'independent' means
jokes.explanation: Dennis's total inability to be alone — going immediately from Mac to Dee as a sidekick — proves the episode's thesis while calling back 'flourishing.' His use of Dee's language ('independent individual') is ironic since he's doing the exact opposite.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, far be it from me to, uh, keep the flower of you from flourishing

jokes.text: "He is... in the wall somewhere."
jokes.setup: Dennis says he's happy to include the cat in movie night
jokes.punchline: Dee casually informs him the cat is 'in the wall somewhere' — delivered with the resigned acceptance of someone who has given up understanding how this happened
jokes.explanation: The ellipsis before 'in the wall somewhere' is doing a lot of work. The absurdity of the cat-in-wall premise is introduced with perfect Dee deadpan. 'Somewhere' implies she's not entirely sure of the location within the wall, adding a layer of helplessness.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Don't do that. I... feel like I'm the one that got us into this mess.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Okay. So you'll stay at Charlie's then.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No. You should stay there... because you already said that you would. Also, I have more stuff.

jokes.text: Dennis's advice on the dead-cat-smell problem: open windows, scented candles, big fan, 'then he'll decompose and everything will be fine. Boom!'
jokes.setup: Dee worries her cat might die in the wall and create a smell
jokes.punchline: Dennis dispenses decomposition-management advice with the confidence of an HGTV host, ending with 'Boom! That's what it's like to have a sidekick. Helped you out of a jam.'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant dark comedy. Dennis's breezy practical advice on managing a decomposing cat — delivered as home-maintenance tips — culminates in him claiming he's 'helped you out of a jam' by telling her how to live with the stench of her dead pet. The 'Boom!' is perfect. Also pays off the 'sidekick/jam' running theme.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Hi. I'm responding to a missing persons report.

jokes.text: Mac to Charlie about trash: 'Why don't you just put your trash into a trash can?' Charlie: 'I put it in the trash can when I'm ready to take it outside, dude.'
jokes.setup: Mac has moved in with Charlie and Frank and is immediately trying to impose order
jokes.punchline: Charlie has an entirely self-consistent but completely insane trash philosophy: the floor is a staging area, the trash can is for when you're ready to go outside
jokes.explanation: Charlie's trash logic is perfectly in character — he has an internal system that is utterly foreign to normal people but makes complete sense to him. The specificity ('when I'm ready to take it outside') is what makes it funny rather than just 'Charlie is messy.'

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Uh, can't do that. He is... in the wall somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: He's in the wall?

jokes.text: "And Jesus Christ, Frank. Are you cutting your toenails with a steak knife?"
jokes.setup: Mac has just discovered Charlie's trash philosophy and is cataloguing the horrors of Charlie and Frank's apartment
jokes.punchline: Frank is cutting his toenails with a steak knife — both a gross visual and an indication of the depths of squalor Mac has entered
jokes.explanation: The 'steak knife toenails' gag is a perfect Frank moment. It escalates the apartment horror and sets up the 'toe knife' running gag that pays off brilliantly later. Frank's complete lack of shame about it is essential.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Or he won't, and he'll die in there, and you'll have a dead cat smell for a while. But listen, I'm gonna help you out of that jam... That's what it's like to have a sidekick. Helped you out of a jam.

jokes.text: "Ah! Oh! Botched toe! I botched that one. Oh, that's a botch job. That's bleeding."
jokes.setup: Frank is cutting toenails with a steak knife
jokes.punchline: He immediately botches a cut, draws blood, and narrates it with the clinical detachment of a surgeon acknowledging an error — 'botched job' as if it's a minor procedural setback, not self-harm
jokes.explanation: Frank's professional vocabulary applied to self-inflicted toenail injury — 'botched job,' 'botched that one' — is very funny. He's not alarmed, he's analytical. Perfectly in character. 'Botched toe' is quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are you cutting your toenails with a steak knife?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I suppose you have a problem with that too?

jokes.text: Frank's solution to the bleeding toe: "I need some trash to plug up the cut." Mac: "Do not plug an open wound with trash." Frank: "Well, it's bleeding like a sieve." Charlie: "Then use your sock, bro." Frank: "Don't waste a good sock on a tiny little cut."
jokes.setup: Frank has cut his toe and needs to stop the bleeding
jokes.punchline: Frank's hierarchy of acceptable wound-plugging materials: trash is acceptable, a sock is wasteful — the inversion of normal hygiene priorities is the joke
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sustained jokes. The escalating negotiation over wound-management materials — trash acceptable, sock wasteful — perfectly encapsulates Frank's deranged priorities. 'Don't waste a good sock on a tiny little cut' is quotable and deeply character-specific. The fact that Mac is horrified while Charlie immediately accepts the sock logic adds layers.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Botched toe! I botched that one. Oh, that's a botch job. That's bleeding. I need some trash to plug up the cut.

jokes.text: "Oh. Oh, wait a minute. That's... That's working. Oh, it's acting like a cut glove."
jokes.setup: Someone has found Frank something to plug the wound with (implied to be trash/candy wrapper)
jokes.punchline: Frank admires the improvisational wound-dressing as 'a cut glove' — he's coined a new term and is delighted by his own ingenuity
jokes.explanation: 'Acting like a cut glove' is a beautiful Frankism — a term he's invented for a thing that shouldn't exist. His satisfaction at having solved the problem with trash is the perfect cap to the wound bit.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Don't waste a good sock on a tiny little cut.

jokes.text: "Ah! Unbelievable, dude. Waste of a sock."
jokes.setup: Mac has apparently insisted on using the sock to clean up after all
jokes.punchline: Frank's genuine outrage at the sock being used — after establishing trash as the superior option — treats the sock waste as a real grievance
jokes.explanation: Good callback. Frank's continued outrage over the sock sustains the bit. 'Waste of a sock' implies he has strong feelings about sock conservation while apparently having no feelings about wound hygiene.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, it's acting like a cut glove.

jokes.text: Mac announces structural changes to Charlie/Frank's apartment: sleeping arrangements, cleaning, etc. Charlie: 'I could use a little structure in my life here.' Mac: 'No, man.' — Frank and Charlie's differing reactions
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to impose domestic order on Charlie and Frank's squalor
jokes.punchline: Charlie, the most squalid of them all, is weirdly receptive ('I could use a little structure') while Mac is the one rejecting the idea, inverting the expected dynamic
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat — Charlie wanting structure is a nice reversal — but it's a minor laugh amid bigger bits in this scene.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are you hearing this shit, bro?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, you know, he's got some good ideas. Maybe it wouldn't be bad if he moved in.

jokes.text: Mac declares Frank should move in because he 'could use a little structure' — Charlie is horrified
jokes.setup: Frank suggests moving in because there's room; Mac surprisingly agrees
jokes.punchline: Mac, who is supposed to be the new organized presence, immediately allies with Frank — the least structured person — against Charlie
jokes.explanation: Setup piece for the Mac-at-Charlie's subplot. The irony of Mac wanting 'structure' and then endorsing Frank is noted but underexploited. Functional transition joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, Mac is being annoying as shit.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, Mac's being annoying? That's a big surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He bossing you around a whole bunch?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Totally bossing me around.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Typical. It's what he does.

jokes.text: Mac's suspicion about who's calling: "Uh... Eh... Is that Dennis?" Charlie: "I don't know who it is. I haven't answered the phone." Mac: "Are you gonna answer it though?"
jokes.setup: A phone is ringing; Mac immediately assumes it's Dennis
jokes.punchline: Mac's hopeful/anxious 'is that Dennis?' — he's been separated for maybe 20 minutes and is already pining — followed by his insistence Charlie answer it
jokes.explanation: Mac's immediate Dennis-fixation after a few minutes of separation is well-observed. His lobbying for Charlie to answer the phone rather than answering it himself is a funny avoidance behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Did he mention me?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No? Really? He didn't say anything at all about me

jokes.text: Phone call between Dennis (at Dee's) and Charlie (at Charlie/Frank's): both complaining about their respective Mac/Dennis problems, then Dennis asks 'Did he mention me?'
jokes.setup: Dennis calls Charlie ostensibly to invite him to movie night at Dee's
jokes.punchline: Within seconds Dennis is asking 'Did he mention me? He didn't say anything at all about me?' — the breakup-ex behavior is fully in effect
jokes.explanation: 'Did he mention me?' is the perfect post-breakup text to receive from an ex. Dennis's desperation — 'He didn't say anything at all about me?' — lands as both funny and pathetic. Very character-specific. The parallel with Mac pining on the other end is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Tell him I'm not talking about him at all. I'm not telling him shit, dude.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, no, Charlie. Don't hang up the phone. I didn't call to talk about Mac. I swear to God, dude.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I could care less about that guy. Are you kidding me?

jokes.text: Mac can be heard in the background yelling 'Is he talking about me?' while Charlie refuses to relay the message; Dennis says 'I could care less about that guy' while clearly caring enormously
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac are both fishing for information about each other through Charlie as intermediary
jokes.punchline: Both are transparently obsessed with the other while maintaining the fiction they don't care; Charlie is caught in the middle of a romantic triangle
jokes.explanation: The two-side-of-a-phone-call structure with Charlie as go-between is excellently executed. Mac yelling 'Is he talking about me?' while Dennis says 'I could care less about that guy' in the same moment is perfectly timed dramatic irony.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He is so annoying. He's always constantly critiquing the fight scenes... and talking about how he could choreograph the fight scenes... so much better than they could, which is ridiculous. He doesn't know shit.

jokes.text: Charlie hangs up and immediately says 'I'll be right over' — Charlie's delight in being included is childlike and immediate
jokes.setup: Mac invites Charlie to Dee's; Dennis and Mac both yell at Charlie to hang up
jokes.punchline: Charlie hangs up and says 'I'll be right over' with zero conflict — he is simply happy to be invited anywhere
jokes.explanation: Good Charlie characterization — his enthusiasm to be included in anything is a consistent trait. The 'yes yes yes' exuberance is in keeping with Charlie's childlike energy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dee, will you forget the goddamn cat for a second... and listen to all the interesting things I have to say? You're being the worst sidekick right now.

jokes.text: Dennis's talking-head: 'I am so excited to watch this movie without Mac. He is so annoying. He's always constantly critiquing the fight scenes and talking about how he could choreograph the fight scenes so much better than they could, which is ridiculous. He doesn't know shit.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has claimed he is enjoying his independence from Mac
jokes.punchline: His entire confessional is about Mac — his complaints, his habits, his incompetence — revealing that Dennis is thinking about nothing but Mac while claiming to be free of him
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony. Dennis's 'I'm so excited to be free of Mac' confessional is entirely about Mac. The specificity of Mac's fight-scene choreography critique is a good detail.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He doesn't like for me to eat the apples with the skin on it. He says the skin's loaded with toxins.

jokes.text: "Ooh! Dennis, I pinpointed him!" Dennis: "Dee, will you forget the goddamn cat for a second and listen to all the interesting things I have to say?"
jokes.setup: Dennis is mid-rant about Mac and his fight-scene critiquing habits
jokes.punchline: Dee interrupts to announce she's located the cat in the wall; Dennis demands she ignore the trapped cat and pay attention to his Mac complaints — 'all the interesting things I have to say'
jokes.explanation: Dennis demanding Dee ignore a trapped animal to hear 'all the interesting things I have to say' is perfectly Dennis — his narcissism treating his Mac gossip as more urgent than animal welfare. The self-description 'interesting things I have to say' is also funny in its self-regard.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I do not like it with the skin, Dee! I'm not allowed to eat it with the skin! I'm not allowed!

jokes.text: "You're being the worst sidekick right now." Dee: "No, you're being the worst sidekick."
jokes.setup: Dennis demanded Dee stop tracking the cat and be his audience
jokes.punchline: Their mutual accusation of being 'the worst sidekick' — both claiming the right to have the other serve as their sidekick simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the sidekick/jam running theme. The mutual 'worst sidekick' accusation is funny and reveals neither of them understands what a sidekick is.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I bet it flattened itself out, went right through a seam in your wall.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't think there's anything in the laws of nature that would support that.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Cats do not abide by the laws of nature, all right?

jokes.text: "But Mac always does it for me." Dee: "Why does Mac peel your apples for you?" Dennis: "He doesn't like for me to eat the apples with the skin on it. He says the skin's loaded with toxins."
jokes.setup: Dee refuses to peel an apple for Dennis
jokes.punchline: Dennis reveals Mac peels his apples because Mac believes apple skin is 'loaded with toxins' — a bizarre health belief that has become a domestic ritual Dennis can no longer perform without
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest jokes. Mac's apple-peeling service for Dennis — predicated on a bro-science belief about skin toxins — perfectly encapsulates their domestic codependency. Dennis cannot eat an apple normally because Mac has restructured his relationship with fruit. The specificity ('loaded with toxins') is what makes it exceptional. High character integration: this could only be Mac and Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm gonna crack a little hole in your wall... Tiny one. It'll be cool. And then I'm gonna slip a second cat in with a string tied around it. Those two will become codependent, then I'll rip the second cat out, and the first one hopefully... hopefully will follow.

jokes.text: "I do not like it with the skin, Dee! I'm not allowed to eat it with the skin! I'm not allowed!"
jokes.setup: Dee tells Dennis to just eat the apple with the skin since Mac isn't here
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not allowed!' — Dennis has internalized Mac's toxin rule so completely that he frames it as a prohibition, as if Mac is an authority figure who governs his apple consumption
jokes.explanation: "I'm not allowed!" is the comedic peak of the apple sequence and one of the best lines in the episode. The escalation from 'Mac peels my apples' to Dennis shrieking 'I'M NOT ALLOWED' as if violating a court order is perfectly calibrated. It's a character revelation, an escalation, and a quotable line simultaneously. Dennis — who considers himself the dominant personality — has accepted complete dietary authority from Mac. The repetition of 'I'm not allowed' hammers it in.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: And I bumped into that guy at the video store. Beefcake? Total jerk-off.

jokes.text: Dee agreeing to peel the apple "the way that Mac likes you to eat it" / "the way that Mac insists"
jokes.setup: Dee has caved and will peel Dennis's apple
jokes.punchline: Her repeated framing — 'the way Mac likes you to eat it,' 'the way Mac insists' — treats Mac as an absent authority figure whose preferences govern the household, which Dee is now enforcing
jokes.explanation: Dee's sarcastic framing extends the apple bit and reinforces how absurd the situation is. Solid callback, slightly less impact than #48 since the peak has already been reached.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: The skin of those things is riddled with toxins! Yeah, get it out though. Get it all out. Yuck! That was a close call. Good save.

jokes.text: Charlie arrives, immediately: "Hey, you want a skinless apple, bud?" Charlie: "Yup." Dennis: "Two skinless apples, Dee. Let's fire the movie up."
jokes.setup: Dee has just been strong-armed into peeling apples Mac's way
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately adopts the skinless apple as his own preference without any context, and Dennis confidently orders two skinless apples from Dee as if she's a waitress
jokes.explanation: Charlie's instant adoption of the skinless apple and Dennis escalating to ordering two is a good escalation of the apple bit. The progression from 'Mac forces this on Dennis' to 'now Dennis is forcing it on Charlie through Dee' is nicely structured.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What... What are you doing now, dude? What?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm taking the toxic skin off.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, but you're cutting it with your toe knife.

jokes.text: "Here's your apple, dick." Dennis: "All right. Yeah." Dennis to Charlie: "Where's mine?" Dee: "You can peel your own apple, Charlie."
jokes.setup: Dee has peeled one apple for Dennis and was asked to peel one for Charlie too
jokes.punchline: Dee hands Dennis his apple with 'Here's your apple, dick' — casual hostility — then refuses Charlie's apple, while Dennis is oblivious to the insult, responding 'All right. Yeah.'
jokes.explanation: Dennis's total unawareness that he's been called a dick — 'All right. Yeah.' — is a good character beat. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So you think not eating cat food is putting on airs?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You betcha!

jokes.text: Charlie: "Cat in the wall, eh? Okay. Now you're talking my language."
jokes.setup: Dee explains the cat is stuck in the wall
jokes.punchline: Charlie treats 'cat in the wall' as a domain he has expertise in — 'now you're talking my language' — as if wall-cat situations are a normal specialty area
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie line. 'Now you're talking my language' implies Charlie has either dealt with wall-cats before or has thought extensively about the scenario. The confidence is completely unjustified and completely in character. High economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Just make sure you, you know, check in. 'Cause I haven't heard from Charlie, and it is getting late.

jokes.text: "I bet it flattened itself out, went right through a seam in your wall." Dee: "I don't think there's anything in the laws of nature that would support that." Charlie: "Cats do not abide by the laws of nature, all right?"
jokes.setup: Charlie is explaining how the cat got into the wall
jokes.punchline: Charlie's theory that the cat flattened itself to slide through a wall seam; when challenged on physical laws, he counters 'Cats do not abide by the laws of nature' — an absurd but delivered-with-conviction statement
jokes.explanation: "Cats do not abide by the laws of nature" is a genuinely great absurdist line. Charlie's total conviction, the specificity of the claim, and Dee's completely reasonable objection make the exchange perfect. The line is quotable, character-specific, and funny on its own as a standalone. This is Charlie at his comedic best — confident expertise in an area where he has no expertise.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Hey, guys! I swallowed apple seeds! ... Are they poisonous?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are you kidding me, dude? They're extremely poisonous!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Should I make myself throw up?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I would throw up now!

jokes.text: Charlie's cat-retrieval plan: crack a hole in the wall, slip a second cat in with a string, 'those two will become codependent, then I'll rip the second cat out, and the first one hopefully... hopefully will follow.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is devising a plan to retrieve the cat from the wall
jokes.punchline: His plan involves engineering feline codependency as a retrieval mechanism — mirroring the episode's Mac/Dennis theme — and the casual 'hopefully... hopefully will follow' betrays that the plan has significant failure modes he is downplaying
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Charlie's retrieval plan — using manufactured cat codependency as a tool — is a perfect thematic mirror of the Mac/Dennis breakup, almost certainly intentional. The plan is insane but internally logical. The 'hopefully... hopefully will follow' hedge is comic genius: it acknowledges the plan's flaw while Charlie still commits to it. The double 'hopefully' is a perfect comedic beat. This joke operates on multiple levels: absurdist comedy, character comedy, and thematic resonance with the episode's central conceit.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Hey, guys! I can't throw up. Should I stick a finger down my throat?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yes!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, my God.

jokes.text: Cats followed Charlie to Dee's apartment: 'I got followed here by, like, 10 cats. Yeah, they're starting to follow me these days.'
jokes.setup: They need a second cat for Charlie's plan
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually mentions he is being followed by approximately 10 cats as a recent development in his life, with no explanation
jokes.explanation: Excellent throwaway Charlie detail — 'they're starting to follow me these days' implies a gradual, unremarked escalation of cat followers in Charlie's life. Very in-character. The casualness of 'these days' is the key comedic word choice.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I got two cats stuck inside this wall. Can't get 'em out. You want to bring in a third? I'm thinking maybe four.

jokes.text: Mac's talking-head: "I got everything... all the groceries, no cat food." Then: "And I bumped into that guy at the video store." Dennis: "Beefcake?" Mac: "Total jerk-off."
jokes.setup: Mac is recounting his errand run to Dennis (they're apparently already back together briefly, or this is a confessional)
jokes.punchline: Dennis has nicknamed the video store clerk 'Beefcake' — a physique-focused nickname — which is funny given Mac's earlier Predator physique obsession; Mac calling him a 'total jerk-off' is jealousy framed as moral judgment
jokes.explanation: Dennis calling the clerk 'Beefcake' is a great detail — given his physique fixation, the nickname makes perfect sense. Mac's instant dismissal 'total jerk-off' is jealousy wearing contempt's clothing. Well-constructed beat.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We work very well together, okay? We're the gruesome twosome!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Gruesome twosome!

jokes.text: Mac arrives at Dee's apartment: "Hey! This place is tits!" Frank: "Yeah, right? Looks good."
jokes.setup: Mac has apparently reconciled with Dennis and arrived at Dee's apartment
jokes.punchline: Mac's enthusiastic 'this place is tits!' — Dee's apartment praised with the highest available compliment — and Frank's satisfied agreement, as if they've accomplished something
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh. 'This place is tits' is a casually vulgar compliment that's slightly funny in context but not a strong joke in itself.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I was told I would be meeting a woman with giant breasts.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I was also told that I was to meet a woman with giant breasts.

jokes.text: Mac sees Frank eating fruit: "Whoa! Frank! No, no! Oh, God, dude! What?" Mac: "The skin of those things is riddled with toxins! Yeah, get it out though. Get it all out. Yuck! Whoo! That was a close call. Good save."
jokes.setup: Frank is eating fruit, presumably with the skin on
jokes.punchline: Mac's horror at the toxin-laden fruit skin — the same belief he imposed on Dennis — now applied universally; Mac physically intervening to remove the toxic fruit from Frank's consumption
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to the apple-skin toxin belief. Mac's panic — 'Oh, God, dude!' / 'The skin of those things is riddled with toxins!' — confirms this is a genuine, deeply-held belief, not just a Dennis-specific quirk. 'That was a close call. Good save.' treats the fruit-skin intervention as a life-saving action. The escalation from 'Mac peels Dennis's apples' to 'Mac physically removes fruit from Frank's hand' is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You son of a bitch!

jokes.text: "Hey, also... I cleaned out this closet. I'm telling you, bro, we could fit a mattress in there. You and Charlie don't have to sleep next to each other anymore."
jokes.setup: Mac has apparently been reorganizing Charlie/Frank's apartment
jokes.punchline: Mac has cleaned out a closet specifically to serve as a bedroom — suggesting Charlie and Frank sleeping in a closet is an improvement over their current arrangement, which requires examination
jokes.explanation: Setup for the 'previous arrangement' joke. The implication that two grown men currently share a sleeping space is more interesting in the follow-up than this setup.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: She looks like a bird.

jokes.text: "Well, I... I kind of liked the other arrangement though. That was pretty good." Mac: "Yeah. The other arrangement was... was not pretty good."
jokes.setup: Mac has proposed separating Charlie and Frank into different sleeping spaces
jokes.punchline: Charlie describes the current arrangement (presumably two grown men sleeping together in squalor) as 'pretty good'; Mac's horrified deadpan correction 'that was not pretty good' implies it was much worse than Charlie realized
jokes.explanation: The ambiguity of 'the arrangement' — what exactly is Charlie's sleeping situation with Frank? — does the comedic work. Mac's traumatized 'that was not pretty good' implies he witnessed something disturbing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Smoke some cigarettes. The smoke will suffocate the bacteria in your stomach.

jokes.text: Mac searching for the word to describe the arrangement: Mac: "It was, um... It was, uh... What... What's the word I'm looking for?" Charlie: "Crazy." Mac: "No, it's not... not crazy. It's like—" Charlie: "Wackadoo." Mac: "No. Just... stop."
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to describe the horror of the sleeping arrangement
jokes.punchline: Charlie's vocabulary assistance — 'crazy,' 'wackadoo' — is both unhelpful and revealing that Charlie doesn't understand why the arrangement was bad, while Mac is so disturbed he can't even name it
jokes.explanation: 'Wackadoo' is a funny word choice from Charlie — it sounds like his vocabulary register, not Mac's. Mac's exasperated 'No. Just... stop.' while trying to process genuine trauma is a good beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: The way they live, bro, it's... it's like, um... it's like...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Preposterous.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, dude! Preposterous! Yeah. I've been trying to come up with that all day!

jokes.text: Mac throws the steak knife out the window. Frank: "Wait. You're throwing my toe knife out?" Mac: "The toe knife is gone." Frank: "Why would you do that?" Mac: "Because you were cutting your fruit with it!" Frank: "What the hell's going on here?"
jokes.setup: Mac has been reorganizing and setting standards in the apartment
jokes.punchline: Frank's naming of the steak knife as 'my toe knife' — having given it an official designation based on its primary use — is the callback. Mac's horror at fruit being cut with the toe knife is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: "My toe knife" is a great coinage — Frank has formally named the knife after its primary function (toenail cutting), and Mac's objection is not that it's a toe knife per se, but that you were 'cutting your fruit with it.' This is an excellent exchange: Frank's possessive relationship with the toe knife, Mac's hierarchy of knife-use hygiene (toe use okay; fruit-and-toe use: unacceptable), and the momentum of the callback all land well.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Like, I'm a man of action, and you're a man that comes up with good... Words? Words, dude! You couldn't think of the word 'words.'

jokes.text: "I'm not gonna put on airs just because I got company." Mac: "So you think not eating cat food is putting on airs?" Frank: "You betcha!"
jokes.setup: Frank is objecting to Mac's domestic improvements and standards
jokes.punchline: Frank considers abstaining from cat food to be an affectation, a performance of sophistication beyond his normal station; "You betcha" delivered with pride
jokes.explanation: "So you think not eating cat food is putting on airs?" / "You betcha!" is a genuinely exceptional exchange. Frank's pride in eating cat food as authentic, non-pretentious behavior is perfect character comedy. 'Putting on airs' is exactly the right phrase — the genteel expression applied to the basest possible dietary standard. 'You betcha!' delivered with conviction is the perfect button. High quotability, superb character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I also was assuming that the big-breasted lady was gonna pay for the drinks, so I don't have any money.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I've got some cash. I can...I can get you out of this jam.

jokes.text: "Look, I gotta take a walk. My head is swimming." Mac: "That's fine. Just make sure you, you know, check in." Charlie: "Oh, my."
jokes.setup: Mac is overwhelmed by the apartment situation and needs to leave
jokes.punchline: Mac automatically tells Charlie to 'check in' — the same behavior that Mac was defending (and that proved codependency) earlier — now applied to Charlie, revealing it's not Dennis-specific, it's just Mac
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character reveal through callback. Mac tells Charlie to 'check in' — the same behavior that defined his codependency with Dennis — proving he applies this to everyone. Charlie's 'Oh, my.' is a perfect reaction: weary amusement. Mac's compulsive check-in demand is a character trait, not a relationship-specific quirk.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I got one. I tied a string around his teeny, tiny little legs. I'm sending it in.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well, congratulations, Dee. You have some very satisfied cats in there, okay?

jokes.text: "Okay, Dee! This little lady is a calico cat. All calico cats are female." Charlie announces this as if the gender fact is relevant and impressive
jokes.setup: Charlie has returned with a second cat to execute his retrieval plan
jokes.punchline: Charlie's announcement that all calico cats are female — delivered as if this is crucial operational information for the cat-retrieval mission — is a mix of genuine cat knowledge and total irrelevance to the task
jokes.explanation: Charlie's confident deployment of the calico gender fact — accurate! — as if it's relevant to wall-cat retrieval is a nice touch. His expertise is real but weirdly applied.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah! Yeah, Deandra! Come on, kitty. Oh. Come on. Okay. I'll get you. I'll get you.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Wow! There are a lot of cats back here!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah. We put a lot of cats in there.

jokes.text: Dee hears something through the wall: "You hear that?" Charlie: "Uh, I hear a squabble." Charlie: "Mm-hmm. It's all part of the dance, okay? They do a little sq... Come on. Wait. Hold on. They do a little—" Dee: "Uh-oh." Charlie: "Crap."
jokes.setup: Charlie has inserted the second cat into the wall to execute his retrieval plan
jokes.punchline: The 'squabble' sounds escalate; Charlie's breezy reassurance ('it's all part of the dance') gives way to 'uh-oh' and 'crap' as the plan immediately goes wrong
jokes.explanation: Charlie's confident 'it's all part of the dance' collapsing into 'crap' when reality intervenes is a good structure. The dance metaphor for cats fighting in a wall is very Charlie. The escalation is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: They're watching Predator. You want to join?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Absolutely, dude.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Great.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah? You guys, I think I'm stuck in the wall.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Guys? Guys? Guys, come on!

jokes.text: "Uh-oh. Crap." — after Charlie inserts the second cat into the wall and they hear a squabble
jokes.setup: Charlie's confident cat-bonding plan is underway; they hear sounds from inside the wall
jokes.punchline: The 'squabble' quickly escalates past 'part of the dance' to something clearly going wrong, and Charlie's minimal 'uh-oh, crap' acknowledges this without any attempt to intervene or explain
jokes.explanation: The minimalism of 'Uh-oh. Crap.' following a confident plan is a solid deadpan beat. The plan has obviously failed immediately, and Charlie's response is entirely inadequate.

jokes.text: "Thanks a lot, Charlie. Goddamn it. I knew I should've gotten a bird."
jokes.setup: Charlie's cat plan has apparently just failed catastrophically
jokes.punchline: Dee's conclusion is that the error was species selection — 'I knew I should've gotten a bird' — implying she had considered birds as wall-extraction tools and rejected them, which is an insane prior thought
jokes.explanation: Dee's regret about the bird implies she had already weighed bird vs. cat for wall-rescue purposes and chose wrong. This is a perfect IASIP line: matter-of-fact delivery of an insane premise as if it's reasonable project management.

jokes.text: "A bird? What are you gonna do with a bird?" Charlie, confused that Dee would use a bird
jokes.setup: Dee announces she should have used a bird
jokes.punchline: Charlie — the man who just stuffed a cat into a wall — is baffled by the bird idea, as if bird deployment is the crazy option here
jokes.explanation: Charlie's incredulity is ironic — he is the last person who should question animal-deployment methodology. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: "Hey, guys! I swallowed apple seeds!" Mac: "So what? Are they poisonous?" Charlie: "Are you kidding me, dude? They're extremely poisonous!" Dee: "They're absolutely not poisonous!" Charlie: "Should I make myself throw up?" Mac: "I would throw up now!"
jokes.setup: In the middle of the cat crisis, Dennis interrupts with an apple seed emergency
jokes.punchline: Complete chaos: Dee correctly says they're not poisonous; Charlie (who doesn't know) says they're extremely poisonous; Mac (who also doesn't know) advises immediate vomiting — the blind leading the blind in an apple seed panic
jokes.explanation: Four people having four different levels of knowledge about apple seed toxicity simultaneously is good farce. The escalation from 'swallowed seeds' to 'make myself throw up' in seconds is very IASIP. The irony that Dee — usually the dumbest one — is the only correct voice is a nice touch.

jokes.text: "Oh, man. We gotta get Mac and Dennis back together, okay? Because they are ruining all of our lives."
jokes.setup: The apple seed panic, two cats in the wall, and general chaos are all happening simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Charlie diagnoses the root cause of all current problems as the Mac/Dennis breakup — and he's correct; the episode's comedic structure makes his logic perfectly valid
jokes.explanation: Charlie's clear-eyed structural diagnosis of the episode's problem is funny because he's completely right. The chaos of their separate lives has been directly caused by Mac and Dennis's breakup. Good meta-awareness from an otherwise chaotic character.

jokes.text: "I got two cats stuck inside this wall. Can't get 'em out." Frank: "You want to bring in a third? I'm thinking maybe four."
jokes.setup: Dee summarizes the wall-cat disaster for Mac
jokes.punchline: Frank's solution to two stuck cats is four cats — a perfectly Frank non-sequitur that doubles down on the failed strategy
jokes.explanation: Frank's immediate escalation to four cats is excellent. He hears the problem statement ('two cats stuck') and his solution is simply more of the same thing that caused the problem. Very Frank. The economy is superb — 'You want to bring in a third? I'm thinking maybe four' is nine words of perfect comedy.

jokes.text: "We work very well together, okay? We're the gruesome twosome! Gruesome twosome!"
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie are being expelled from the cat situation for making it worse
jokes.punchline: Frank declares their partnership as 'the gruesome twosome' with the enthusiasm of someone announcing a superhero duo — framing their catastrophic cat wall-stuffing as teamwork excellence
jokes.explanation: "Gruesome twosome" mirrors the "dynamic duo" callback: Frank and Charlie form their own codependent partnership as a parallel to Mac and Dennis. The enthusiasm of the declaration is proportional to the failure that preceded it. Good thematic symmetry.

jokes.text: "What? He swallowed some apple seeds." — Dee's flat explanation for why Dennis needs medical attention
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are trying to manage the Mac/Dennis reunion; Dennis has apparently been taken to some medical setting
jokes.punchline: Dee's matter-of-fact 'He swallowed some apple seeds' as the reason for the medical situation — the mundane absurdity of the apple seed panic requiring attention
jokes.explanation: Good economy. Dee's flat delivery of the apple seed explanation treats it as routine, which is funny. Brief transitional joke.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis meet at a bar, each believing they've been set up with 'a woman with giant breasts.' Both delivered with equal excitement and disappointment.
jokes.setup: Dee has separately told each of them she's setting them up with 'a woman with giant breasts'
jokes.punchline: Both arrive expecting a buxom woman and find each other — Dee has set them up on a date with each other
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom reunion structure with a good twist. Using the 'giant breasts' bait is very Dee — practical and crude. The 'I was also told I was to meet a woman with giant breasts' mirroring is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Dee: "Yes, geniuses. I set you up. Now, can you please make up, because you're driving everyone crazy." Then: "I think you have a great friendship, and it's perfectly natural for two grown men to need each other this badly."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have just realized Dee tricked them into meeting each other
jokes.punchline: Dee's apology for calling them codependent pivots immediately into 'it's perfectly natural for two grown men to need each other this badly' — which is not an apology but a condescending affirmation that also confirms the codependency
jokes.explanation: 'It's perfectly natural for two grown men to need each other this badly' reads as a sincere apology on the surface and an absolute roast on second reading. Dee lands the insult while technically making peace. Good economy.

jokes.text: Mac starts to say something conciliatory... then yells: "You son of a bitch!" — apparently seeing or realizing something about Dennis
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are supposedly in the process of making up
jokes.punchline: The reconciliation is interrupted by Mac suddenly calling Dennis a son of a bitch — whatever Dennis did or said in that moment is enough to restart the fight immediately
jokes.explanation: The speed of the relapse — mid-reconciliation speech to 'you son of a bitch' — is very funny. It undermines the entire setup-the-reunion plot and suggests their relationship is simply incompatible with peace. The abruptness is the joke.

jokes.text: "I don't care anymore. Guess what? Neither one of you are ever going into my apartment ever again, okay? So make up, don't make up, kill each other... I don't care. I need to go get a bird."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have immediately resumed fighting mid-reconciliation attempt
jokes.punchline: Dee exits with 'I need to go get a bird' — the bird is her actual priority and the Mac/Dennis situation is beneath her concern in comparison
jokes.explanation: Perfect character exit. The cascade from 'I don't care' → 'make up, don't make up, kill each other' → 'I need to go get a bird' is an excellent escalation. The bird callback lands here because the bird was established as an absurd but earnest solution to a different problem. Dee prioritizing bird acquisition over human relationships is funny and in character.

jokes.text: Mac watching Dee leave: "She looks like a bird."
jokes.setup: Dee has just dramatically exited
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'She looks like a bird' is the return of the running bird-insult gag from the opening scene — now deployed as a parting shot with zero ceremony
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. The callback to the opening scene bird insult — timed perfectly after Dee announces she needs to 'get a bird' — lands as a comedic double. The timing is impeccable. Pure economy.

jokes.text: "I swallowed some apple seeds today." Dennis's doctor: "Did you make yourself throw up?" Dennis: "I tried, but I couldn't." Doctor: "Smoke some cigarettes. The smoke will suffocate the bacteria in your stomach."
jokes.setup: Dennis has apparently gone to see a medical professional about swallowing apple seeds
jokes.punchline: The 'doctor' advises smoking cigarettes to 'suffocate the bacteria' — pseudoscientific medicine delivered with professional confidence; also, apple seeds contain cyanide precursors, not bacteria
jokes.explanation: The 'doctor' (probably not a real doctor) dispensing cigarette therapy for accidental fruit ingestion is a great dark comedy beat. 'Suffocate the bacteria in your stomach' is hilariously specific bad medicine. The whole thing implies Dennis went to some kind of sketchy medical practitioner, which is very IASIP.

jokes.text: Mac's post-separation assessment of Charlie's apartment: "The way they live, bro, it's... It's like, um... It's like... Preposterous."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are apparently reuniting; Mac is recounting his time at Charlie's
jokes.punchline: Mac's vocabulary fails him ('it's like... um... it's like...') and the best he can produce is 'preposterous' — a word that undersells what we know to be the actual horror of Charlie/Frank's apartment
jokes.explanation: Mac struggling to find the word and landing on 'preposterous' is funny because we know exactly how bad Charlie's apartment is — toenail knives, cat food, floor trash — and 'preposterous' is hilariously inadequate.

jokes.text: "You really gotta work on your vocabulary though, man." Mac: "Well, you could help me. You couldn't think of the word 'words.'"
jokes.setup: Dennis has just praised Mac and himself as a great team
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately criticizes Mac's vocabulary; Mac points out Dennis couldn't supply the word 'words' — the perfect counter that Dennis has no defense against
jokes.explanation: "You couldn't think of the word 'words'" is a devastating and perfectly timed comeback. It immediately undercuts Dennis's superiority position. The callback lands perfectly — the audience just saw it happen. Good structure, excellent economy.

jokes.text: Bartender reveals Dennis has had six rum and Cokes, not 'a couple'
jokes.setup: Mac says Mac's being annoying; Dennis mentions he had 'a couple' of drinks while nervous about the big-breasted woman
jokes.punchline: 'Six, actually' — Dennis had six rum and Cokes because he was nervous about meeting a woman, which reveals his insecurity under the narcissism
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom correction joke — 'a couple' corrected to 'six' — but elevated by Dennis's admission of nervousness about an attractive woman, which undercuts his usual pomposity. Functional and well-timed.

jokes.text: "Now might be a good time for you to pay your bill and leave." Dennis: "Well, you're not making sense 'cause we didn't buy anything." Mac: "Actually, I... Oh." Bartender: "I had a couple of rum and Cokes." Mac: "You had six, actually." Mac: "Six? I had six of 'em."
jokes.setup: The bartender asks them to pay their bill
jokes.punchline: Dennis claims they didn't buy anything; Mac admits he had 'a couple'; the bartender corrects him to six — the anxiety drinking escalation revealed
jokes.explanation: Mac's anxious drinking — 'a couple' revealed as six — is a good character beat. Dennis's confident 'we didn't buy anything' being immediately wrong adds a nice layer.

jokes.text: "Did you? Yeah. I was nervous about the big-breasted lady." Dennis: "I was nervous about her too. You got nervous too?" Mac: "A beautiful woman. Dee said she had giant boobs, you know? I'm really excited about it."
jokes.setup: Mac reveals he drank six rum and Cokes because he was nervous about meeting the big-breasted woman
jokes.punchline: Both admit they were nervous about the fictional woman — but Mac is apparently still excited about her arrival, unaware she was always fictional
jokes.explanation: Their shared anxiety about a woman neither of them can identify as fictional — given they've already found each other — is a good beat that gently plays on their self-delusion.

jokes.text: "I was also assuming that the big-breasted lady was gonna pay for the drinks, so I don't have any money." Mac: "I've got some cash. I can... I can get you out of this jam."
jokes.setup: They need to pay for Mac's six drinks; Dennis has no money
jokes.punchline: Mac covering the bill and framing it as getting Dennis out of a 'jam' — the callback to the episode's running 'jam' motif — lands perfectly as the reunion's first act of partnership
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to the 'jam' motif established in the opening scene. The episode began with Mac and Dennis arguing that they needed each other to handle potential jams; now Mac demonstrates this by literally getting Dennis out of a jam (a bar bill he can't pay). The structure is elegant: the comedy and the theme converge. Dennis's assumption that a fictional woman would pay for his drinks is also funny on its own.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I've got some cash. I can get you out of this jam.' — echoing the 'jam' language from Mac's earlier reasoning for always being together
jokes.setup: Mac has no money; Dennis offers to cover
jokes.punchline: 'I can get you out of this jam' — the exact justification Mac used for why they should always travel together now proven correct in a micro way
jokes.explanation: Perfect thematic callback — the 'jam' language from their very first scene returns as genuine vindication. Mac said they needed each other in case of jams; Dennis pays his bar tab. The episode proves their codependency is at least functionally useful. Well-constructed structural payoff.

jokes.text: "Watch your eyes." — heard through the wall as Frank and Charlie bash a large hole in Dee's apartment
jokes.setup: Dee thought she had resolved the cat situation and expelled Frank and Charlie
jokes.punchline: Frank and Charlie have returned and are now smashing a large hole in Dee's wall — the 'tiny hole' Charlie proposed has become a large-scale demolition
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'tiny hole' to full demolition is well-structured. 'Watch your eyes' as the only warning before a large hole is broken in someone else's wall is a good Frank/Charlie moment.

jokes.text: "Yeah. We're bashing a bigger hole in your wall." Dee: "Yeah, I see that." Frank: "We're gonna stuff all the cats in at one time."
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie have broken a large hole in Dee's wall
jokes.punchline: Frank's plan is now to 'stuff all the cats in at one time' — a plan so wrong it circles back around to being a plan, sort of
jokes.explanation: Frank explaining his plan with total confidence despite it making no sense is very Frank. The escalation from one cat to two to 'all the cats at one time' is well-paced.

jokes.text: "No more big holes in my wall, no more cats. We're doing the bird thing. I got one. I tied a string around his teeny, tiny little legs. I'm sending it in."
jokes.setup: Dee overrules the cat strategy
jokes.punchline: Dee has acquired a bird, tied a string to its legs (animal welfare implications aside), and is about to deploy it into the wall — the bird plan from earlier, now fully operational
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the 'I should've gotten a bird' callback. Dee has actually done it. 'Teeny, tiny little legs' is a great detail — she's describing the bird with affection while preparing to use it as a retrieval tool. The string around its legs implies she's thought about the extraction mechanism. Good character work.

jokes.text: Bird is tossed into the wall hole, brief sounds of chaos, then: "Well, congratulations, Dee. You have some very satisfied cats in there, okay?"
jokes.setup: Dee has thrown a bird into the wall to retrieve the cats
jokes.punchline: Charlie's deadpan 'you have some very satisfied cats in there' implies the cats have eaten the bird — dark, delivered with the clinical detachment of a wildlife observer reporting facts
jokes.explanation: "You have some very satisfied cats in there" is an exceptional dark comedy line. Charlie's completely neutral delivery of the news that the cats have eaten Dee's bird — the bird she just acquired, the one she tied a string to — is devastating. The euphemism 'very satisfied' does enormous work. The structure is perfect: Dee's hopeful bird plan → chaos sounds → Charlie's clinical verdict. High dark comedy impact.

jokes.text: "Deandra, we're out of here. Yeah." Frank and Charlie receive a text that Mac and Dennis are back together watching Predator, and immediately abandon Dee.
jokes.setup: Dee is in the middle of a wall cat/bird crisis
jokes.punchline: The moment a better option (Predator with Mac and Dennis) becomes available, Frank and Charlie immediately abandon Dee without a second thought
jokes.explanation: Good IASIP character beat — everyone abandons Dee the moment they don't need her. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "That's why she needs a friend. You gotta have a sidekick. That's all I'm saying."
jokes.setup: Dee is stuck in the wall as Mac and Dennis prepare to leave
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers the episode's moral — 'you gotta have a sidekick' — as a callback to the running 'sidekick/jam' motif, using Dee's predicament as proof of concept
jokes.explanation: The thematic button of the episode. Dennis uses 'sidekick' — the word that has run through the entire episode — to summarize the lesson while Dee is literally stuck in a wall. The irony that the codependent duo is teaching the lesson about needing a partner while Dee (who called them pathetic) is now the proof of their thesis is perfectly structured. High structural score for bringing the episode's themes home.

jokes.text: "You guys, I think I'm stuck in the wall." Frank and Charlie exit. Final scene: Dee is stuck in the wall, calling "Guys? Guys? Guys, come on!" as everyone leaves.
jokes.setup: Dee has gone into the wall herself to retrieve the cats
jokes.punchline: She is now stuck in the wall — the third entity to become trapped — as everyone abandons her exactly as they warned her they would
jokes.explanation: The perfect IASIP tag. Dee — who mocked Mac and Dennis for needing each other — ends the episode literally stuck in a wall, alone, calling for help while everyone ignores her. The comedy and the theme converge: the episode's thesis is that everyone needs someone, and Dee (who denied this) is the one who ends up alone and trapped. Structurally it's flawless: the final joke pays off multiple threads (the wall, Dee's loneliness, the spinster insults). Dennis's callback — 'That's why she needs a friend. You gotta have a sidekick' — is the thesis bow. Highest structural score in the episode.

jokes.text: Dee, still in the wall: 'Guys? Guys? Guys, come on!' — left behind by everyone
jokes.setup: Everyone has left; Dee is physically stuck in her own wall
jokes.punchline: The final image of the episode — Dee alone, calling out to friends who are already gone, literally trapped — is the dark comedic thesis made physical
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. Dee started the episode introducing a cat because she had no one to talk to. She ends it physically trapped in a wall, calling after people who have already left. The visual metaphor for her isolation is perfectly constructed and completely earned. The 'Guys? Guys? Guys, come on!' with diminishing hope is a great cold-end beat. Earns 8+ for structural elegance and total earned comedy.

tmdb_overview: Mac and Dennis decide that they need to spend some time away from each other. Meanwhile, Charlie helps Dee search for her cat.
